lineas.texto: Part Three. You will hear five short extracts in which people talk about moving to a different town. For questions one to five, choose from the list A to H what each speaker says. Use each letter only once. There are three extra letters which you do not need to use.

I would not have gone if it had been up to me, and I want to be honest about that because people tell the story afterwards as though it was a shared adventure. Her job was in Leeds, my job could be done anywhere, and so we went to Leeds. It has worked out. But the decision was hers and I made it easier, and those are two different things.

The advertisement said I would be running a department. I arrived and there was no department: there was me, a filing cabinet and a plan to build one at some point in the next two years. Nobody had lied exactly, they had just described the intention rather than the situation. I stayed eighteen months, which was longer than it deserved, and I would ask much harder questions now.

For the first four months I spoke to nobody except at work, and I had begun to think the place was unfriendly, which it is not. Then I joined the choir at the church hall, which I had walked past three hundred times. Within a month I knew forty people. It sounds like the sort of advice you would ignore, and it was the only thing that worked.

The flat is bigger, the neighbours are kind and the work is better paid. What nobody prepares you for is the light. Where I grew up it rains and it is grey, and I complained about it constantly for twenty-nine years, and now I live somewhere warm and I miss it in a way I cannot defend and cannot stop.

I had budgeted for a disaster. I put aside six months of savings, took the cheapest flat I could find and prepared to be miserable about money for a year. Then the rent was two-thirds of what I had been paying, the bus was a euro, and by March I had more in the account than when I arrived. I am still slightly suspicious of it.
That is the end of Part Three.
